body.statement: There is a finite constant \(C<\infty\), depending only on \((d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), such that the total estimator \(\widehat\tau_n(0)\) satisfies \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)}\mathbb E_{P_O^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\tau_n(0)-\tau_P(0)|\le C\rho_n\] for every \(n\ge2\). More precisely, with \(\ell_n=h_n/M_n\) and \(K_n\asymp M_n^d\), its risk is at most \(C\{h_n^\gamma+\ell_n^S+(nh_n^d)^{-1/2}+\sqrt{K_n}/(nh_n^d)\}\).
body.justification: A same-class converse is informative only when paired with a finite estimator that attains the candidate order on every data set.
body.gap: KennedyBalakrishnanRobinsWasserman2024MinimaxCATE supplies the higher-order upper architecture; this theorem records its exact-known-uniform, one-sided, total finite specialization and does not claim the exponent as a new upper rate.
body.consumer: The theorem gives an implementable precision benchmark for observational CATE workflows that estimate outcome and propensity regressions.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), and abbreviate \(e=e_P\), \(\mu_0=\mu_{0,P}\), and \(\tau=\tau_P\).  All constants below are uniform in \(P\) and may depend only on \((d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  Put \(D_0=[0,1]^d\), \(h=h_n\), \(M=M_n\), \(K=K_n\), and \(\ell=h/M\).  Let \(\Pi_M\) denote coordinatewise Lebesgue orthogonal projection on the piecewise-polynomial space generated by \(b_{M_n}\).  Thus, by the exact Gram identity in \(\mathrm{def:corrected\mbox{-}moments}\),
\[
(\Pi_M u)(z)=b_{M_n}(z)^{\mathsf T}\int_{D_0}b_{M_n}(z')u(z')\,dz',
\qquad \|\Pi_Mu\|_2\le \|u\|_2.
\]
The projection is applied to each coordinate when \(u\) is vector-valued.

We first record the deterministic approximation facts used below.  If \(r>0\), \(m_r=\lceil r\rceil-1\), and \(u\in\mathcal H_d^r(L)\), restriction of \(u\) to a line segment followed by the one-dimensional Taylor formula gives, on every cube of side \(\ell\), a polynomial \(T\) of degree at most \(m_r\) satisfying
\[
\sup_x|u(x)-T(x)|\le C\ell^r.
\]
Indeed, the integral remainder is bounded by the stated order-\(m_r\) H\"older seminorm; when \(r\) is an integer, the exponent in the frozen definition is one and gives the same bound.  Applying this cell by cell after the change of variables \(x=hz\), and using the best-approximation property of \(\Pi_M\), yields
\[
\begin{split}
\|(I-\Pi_M)\{v_j(e(h\,\cdot)-3/8)\}\|_2&\le C\ell^\alpha,\\
\|(I-\Pi_M)\{v_j e(h\,\cdot)\}\|_2&\le C\ell^\alpha,\\
\|(I-\Pi_M)\{\mu_0(h\,\cdot)-1/2\}\|_2&\le C\ell^\beta.
\end{split} \tag{1}
\]
For the first two inequalities, multiply the cellwise Taylor polynomial of \(e\) by \(v_j\).  Its degree is at most \(m_\alpha+m_\gamma\le p_{\mathrm{deg}}\), so it belongs to the specified projection space.  For the third, \(m_\beta\le p_{\mathrm{deg}}\).  This proves (1) directly from \(\mathrm{ass:propensity\mbox{-}holder}\), \(\mathrm{ass:control\mbox{-}holder}\), and the definition of the two bases.

Write \(e_h(z)=e(hz)\), \(\tau_h^0(z)=\tau(hz)\), and define
\[
Q=\int_{D_0}v(z)v(z)^{\mathsf T}e_h(z)\{1-e_h(z)\}\,dz,
\qquad
R=\int_{D_0}v(z)e_h(z)\{1-e_h(z)\}\tau_h^0(z)\,dz.
\]
The propensity-envelope and propensity-normalization assumptions imply \(1/4\le e_h\le1/2\).  Since \(v\) is Lebesgue orthonormal,
\[
u^{\mathsf T}Qu\ge \frac{3}{16}\int_{D_0}\{u^{\mathsf T}v(z)\}^2dz
=\lambda_0\|u\|_2^2,
\qquad \lambda_0=3/16. \tag{2}
\]
Hence \(Q\) is invertible.  Put \(\theta=Q^{-1}R\) and \(\tau_h^\star(hz)=v(z)^{\mathsf T}\theta\).  The response-interiority assumption gives \(|\tau|\le3/4\); consequently (2), boundedness of \(e_h\) and \(v\), and the definition of \(R\) imply \(\|\theta\|_2\le C\).  The line-segment Taylor argument above supplies a polynomial \(t\) of degree at most \(m_\gamma\) with
\[
\sup_{z\in D_0}|t(z)-\tau(hz)|\le Ch^\gamma.
\]
If \(\theta_t\) is its coefficient vector in the \(v\)-basis, then (2), boundedness of the fixed-dimensional vector \(v\), and the normal equations give
\[
\|\theta-\theta_t\|_2
\le \|Q^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\left\|\int_{D_0}v e_h(1-e_h)(\tau_h^0-t)\right\|_2
\le Ch^\gamma.
\]
Consequently
\[
\sup_{z\in D_0}|\tau_h^\star(hz)-\tau(hz)|\le Ch^\gamma,
\qquad
|v(0)^{\mathsf T}\theta-\tau(0)|\le Ch^\gamma. \tag{3}
\]

We next compute the population corrected moments rather than postulating their bias.  Put \(p=3/8\), \(\delta_e=e_h-p\), and \(\delta_\mu=\mu_0(h\,\cdot)-1/2\).  Conditional Bernoulli calculation gives
\[
\mathbb E[A(A-p)\mid X=hz]=e_h(z)(1-p),
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-1/2)(A-p)\mid X=hz]
=\delta_e(z)\delta_\mu(z)+e_h(z)(1-p)\tau_h^0(z). \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, \(\mathbb E[A\mid X=hz]=e_h(z)\), \(\mathbb E[A-p\mid X=hz]=\delta_e(z)\), and
\[
\mathbb E[Y-1/2\mid X=hz]=\delta_\mu(z)+e_h(z)\tau_h^0(z). \tag{5}
\]
The exact uniform design, the factors \(h^{-d}\), independence for \(i\ne j\), and (4)--(5) therefore yield, with \(\overline Q=\mathbb E_P\widetilde Q_n\) and \(\overline R=\mathbb E_P\widetilde R_n\),
\[
\begin{split}
\overline Q
&=\int v v^{\mathsf T}e_h(1-p)
-\int \Pi_M(v\delta_e)e_hv^{\mathsf T},\\
\overline R
&=\int v\{\delta_e\delta_\mu+e_h(1-p)\tau_h^0\}
-\int \Pi_M(v\delta_e)\{\delta_\mu+e_h\tau_h^0\},
\end{split} \tag{6}
\]
where every unmarked integral in this proof is over \(D_0\).  Projection orthogonality changes the first difference in (6) into
\[
\overline Q-Q
=\int (I-\Pi_M)(v\delta_e)\,(I-\Pi_M)(e_hv)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Thus (1) and Cauchy--Schwarz show
\[
\|\overline Q-Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\ell^{2\alpha}. \tag{7}
\]
Let \(\Delta=\tau_h^0-v^{\mathsf T}\theta\).  Subtracting \(\overline Q\theta\) from \(\overline R\) in (6), adding and subtracting \(v\delta_e e_h\Delta\), and again using projection orthogonality gives the exact identity
\[
\overline R-\overline Q\theta
=\int (I-\Pi_M)(v\delta_e)(I-\Pi_M)(\delta_\mu+e_h\Delta)
+\int v e_h(1-e_h)\Delta. \tag{8}
\]
The last integral is zero by \(Q\theta=R\).  Equations (1), (3), projection contraction, and Cauchy--Schwarz now imply
\[
\|\overline R-\overline Q\theta\|_2
\le C\{\ell^{\alpha+\beta}+\ell^\alpha h^\gamma\}
\le C(\ell^S+h^\gamma). \tag{9}
\]

It remains to control sampling fluctuation.  Every coordinate of the empirical first-order terms has second moment at most \(Ch^{-d}\), because \(A,Y\) and the fixed-dimensional vector \(v\) are bounded and
\[
\int_{hD_0}h^{-2d}\,dx=h^{-d}.
\]
For the ordered pair terms, put \(k_M(z,z')=b_{M_n}(z)^{\mathsf T}b_{M_n}(z')\).  Orthonormality gives
\[
\int_{D_0}\int_{D_0}k_M(z,z')^2\,dz\,dz'=K. \tag{10}
\]
Hence a full two-index kernel has squared \(L^2\) norm at most \(CKh^{-2d}\).  Conditional integration over either one of its indices produces an orthogonal projection of one of the bounded functions in (4)--(5); projection contraction then bounds the squared \(L^2\) norm of every one-index projection by \(Ch^{-d}\).  Expanding the variance of the ordered sum makes terms with four distinct indices vanish by \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}sampling}\).  There are at most \(Cn^3\) ordered pairs of kernels sharing one index and at most \(Cn^2\) sharing two.  Dividing by \(n^2(n-1)^2\), and using (10), proves
\[
\mathbb E_P\|\widetilde Q_n-\overline Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
+\mathbb E_P\|\widetilde R_n-\overline R\|_2^2
\le C\left\{\frac1{nh^d}+\frac K{n^2h^{2d}}\right\}=:CV_n^2. \tag{11}
\]
The replacement of coordinatewise Euclidean norms by the operator norm costs only a constant because \(q\) is fixed.

Since \(\ell\to0\), (7) is at most \(\lambda_0/4\) for all \(n\ge n_0\), where \(n_0\) depends only on the fixed parameters.  On
\[
\mathcal E_n=\{\|\widetilde Q_n-\overline Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\lambda_0/4\},
\]
(2) and (7) imply \(s_{\min}(\widetilde Q_n)\ge\lambda_0/2\).  Thus the inverse branch of \(\mathrm{def:total\mbox{-}estimator}\) is used and \(\|\widetilde Q_n^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2/\lambda_0\).  Clipping cannot increase distance to \(\tau(0)\in[-3/4,3/4]\).  From (3), (9), and (11), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\mathbb E_P[|\widehat\tau_n(0)-\tau(0)|\mathbf1_{\mathcal E_n}]
\le C\{h^\gamma+\ell^S+V_n\}. \tag{12}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_n^c\), both the clipped estimator and the target lie in \([-3/4,3/4]\).  Chebyshev's inequality and (11) give
\[
\mathbb E_P[|\widehat\tau_n(0)-\tau(0)|\mathbf1_{\mathcal E_n^c}]
\le \frac32\min\{1,CV_n^2\}\le CV_n. \tag{13}
\]
Combining (12)--(13), and enlarging the constant over the finitely many \(2\le n<n_0\), proves the advertised nonasymptotic envelope
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)}
\mathbb E_P|\widehat\tau_n(0)-\tau_P(0)|
\le C\left\{h_n^\gamma+\ell_n^S+(nh_n^d)^{-1/2}
+\frac{\sqrt{K_n}}{nh_n^d}\right\}. \tag{14}
\]
The finite enlargement is legitimate because \(n_0\) is fixed and the loss is at most \(3/2\).

Finally, \(S<S_\star<\gamma\), so \(x_n=n^{\eta(1/S-1/\gamma)}\ge1\) and
\[
x_n\le M_n=\lceil x_n\rceil\le2x_n,
\qquad
\tfrac12n^{-\eta/S}\le\ell_n\le n^{-\eta/S},
\qquad K_n\le Cn^{\eta d(1/S-1/\gamma)}. \tag{15}
\]
The definitions of \(\eta\) and \(h_n\) give
\[
h_n^\gamma=n^{-\eta},\qquad \ell_n^S\le n^{-\eta},
\qquad
\frac{\sqrt{K_n}}{nh_n^d}
\le Cn^{-1+\eta d/(2S)+\eta d/(2\gamma)}=Cn^{-\eta}. \tag{16}
\]
Also
\[
(nh_n^d)^{-1/2}\le n^{-\eta}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S\le\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}, \tag{17}
\]
which follows from \(\mathrm{ass:below\mbox{-}elbow}\).  Substitution of (16)--(17) into (14) proves the claimed \(C\rho_n\) bound for every \(n\ge2\).  The half-open cells, finite sums, continuous singular values, measurable branch, matrix inversion on the nonsingular branch, and clipping also show directly that \(\widehat\tau_n(0)\) is a total finite Borel map, as required.
